title: Senator Padilla Renews Push for Green Card Bill That Could Benefit Millions of H-1B Workers
excerpt: The California Democrat's legislation would replace the Immigration Registry's 1972 cutoff with a rolling seven-year residency requirement, potentially opening a pathway for over 8 million long-term residents.
body:
• California Senator Alex Padilla has renewed his push for a bill that would replace the Immigration Registry's fixed January 1, 1972 cutoff with a rolling seven-year continuous residency requirement, potentially opening a green card pathway for over 8 million people.
  • Indian H-1B professionals, who make up roughly 80% of the employment-based green card backlog, are among the groups that could benefit, though the bill remains in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no Republican support.
  • The bill is co-led by Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin with 14 co-sponsors, and a companion bill has been introduced in the House by Rep. Zoe Lofgren.
  • Between 2015 and 2019, only 305 people adjusted their status under the current Registry provision, underscoring how outdated the existing cutoff has become.

Senator Alex Padilla of California reiterated his support on July 27 for legislation that would overhaul a century-old immigration provision and create a green card pathway for millions of long-term U.S. residents, including tens of thousands of Indian H-1B visa holders stuck in employment-based backlogs stretching decades into the future.

What the Bill Proposes

The Renewing Immigration Provisions of the Immigration Act of 1929 targets Section 249 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, known as the Registry provision. The Registry allows immigrants who entered the U.S. before a specified cutoff date to apply for lawful permanent resident status, provided they demonstrate good moral character and continuous residence.

The problem: Congress last updated the cutoff in 1986 during the Reagan administration, setting it at January 1, 1972. That date is now more than 54 years in the past, rendering the provision effectively useless — only 305 people adjusted status under it between 2015 and 2019, according to Padilla's office.

Padilla's bill would replace the fixed cutoff with a rolling seven-year requirement. Anyone who has lived continuously in the United States for at least seven years before filing would be eligible to apply for permanent residency. The change would take effect 60 days after enactment.

"Congress cannot continue to ignore millions of long-term residents who contribute to our economy and communities every day. It's past time to modernise our immigration laws and create a fair pathway to lawful permanent residency."

— Senator Alex Padilla (D-CA)

Who Could Benefit

Padilla's office estimates the legislation could open a pathway for more than 8 million people. The groups cited include Dreamers — undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children — Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders, essential workers, children of long-term visa holders who age out of dependent status after turning 21, and highly skilled professionals on H-1B visas who have been waiting years for employment-based visa numbers.

The bill would not grant automatic green cards. Applicants would still need to go through the Registry process, pass criminal and national security background checks, and meet existing eligibility requirements. The Department of Homeland Security would retain discretion over individual cases.

The Indian H-1B Backlog

The legislation carries particular significance for Indian professionals in the U.S. immigration pipeline. Indians account for roughly 70% of the approximately 85,000 H-1B visas issued annually and make up an estimated 80% of the pending employment-based green card backlog, according to immigration advocacy groups. Due to per-country visa caps that limit any single nation to 7% of annual allotments, wait times for Indian applicants are estimated at 15 years to several decades.

While the Registry bill does not directly address per-country caps — the core structural problem driving the Indian backlog — it could provide an alternative pathway for H-1B holders who have maintained continuous U.S. residence for seven or more years, a threshold many long-term workers would meet.

Political Prospects

The bill, designated S. 2468 and introduced on July 28, 2025, is co-led by Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin and carries 14 additional co-sponsors, including Senators Cory Booker, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Adam Schiff, and Tammy Duckworth. A companion bill has been introduced in the House by Representative Zoe Lofgren of California. Over 30 organizations have endorsed the measure.

However, the legislation faces steep odds. It remains in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no Republican co-sponsors, and the current Congress has shown little appetite for immigration liberalization. The Dignity Act, a bipartisan immigration reform bill introduced in the House, has also stalled. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been tightening immigration enforcement, with recent executive orders restricting birthright citizenship and expanded ICE operations targeting immigrant communities.

What to Watch

With Republicans controlling both chambers and the Trump administration actively pursuing restrictionist immigration policies, the bill is unlikely to advance in its current form. But it serves as a legislative marker — the latest in a long line of Democratic attempts to modernize the Registry provision. If political dynamics shift, the rolling cutoff mechanism could become a template for future bipartisan negotiations on immigration reform. For the estimated one million Indian professionals waiting in the green card queue, any movement toward reducing backlogs remains closely watched.
